questions.q: Which combination of SI base units is equivalent to one joule?
o: That is the newton, a unit of force, not energy.
That is the watt (J/s), a unit of power.
That is the unit of momentum or impulse.
questions.x: Energy is force times distance, so a joule is a newton-meter. Expanding the newton (kg·m/s²) and multiplying by meters gives kg·m²/s². The tempting kg·m²/s³ has one extra factor of 1/s, which turns energy into energy per time: power in watts.

questions.q: A quantity is calculated as (force × time) ÷ mass. What are its SI units?
o: Drops the factor of time; F/m alone would be an acceleration.
Force × time is impulse, but the division by mass was skipped.
Correct: (kg·m/s² × s) ÷ kg = m/s, a velocity (impulse ÷ mass).
Adds an extra factor of seconds; the result is velocity, not length.
questions.note: Impulse ÷ mass = change in velocity.
questions.x: Force times time is impulse, which equals the change in momentum (kg·m/s). Dividing momentum by mass leaves velocity, m/s. Stopping at N·s forgets the division by mass; tracking each unit through every operation avoids this.

questions.q: A spring constant k (from F = −kx) has SI units equivalent to:
o: That is a newton; k is force per unit length.
Missing one factor of 1/s from the newton.
That is a joule; k is not an energy.
questions.x: From F = −kx, k = F/x, so its units are newtons per meter. Writing the newton as kg·m/s² and cancelling the meter leaves kg/s². This also fits ω = √(k/m): k/m has units 1/s², a squared angular frequency.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT an SI base unit?
o: The kilogram is the SI base unit of mass.
Correct: the newton is derived, kg·m/s².
The kelvin is the SI base unit of temperature.
The ampere is the SI base unit of electric current.
questions.x: The seven SI base units are the meter, kilogram, second, ampere, kelvin, mole and candela. Every other unit, such as the newton, joule, watt, pascal and coulomb, is built from them. The newton is kg·m/s², from F = ma.

questions.q: Stokes' law gives drag on a small sphere as F = 6πηrv. What are the SI units of the viscosity η?
o: That is momentum; it treats η as F × time.
That is pressure; the velocity term contributes an extra second.
Correct: η = F/(rv) = (kg·m/s²)/(m·m/s) = kg/(m·s), i.e., Pa·s.
Divides force by velocity only, ignoring the radius.
questions.note: η is often written Pa·s.
questions.x: Rearrange Stokes' law so η = F/(6πrv). The 6π has no units, so η = N ÷ (m·m/s) = (kg·m/s²)·s/m² = kg/(m·s), which is the same as Pa·s. N/m² is tempting, but it leaves out the extra second that comes from dividing by velocity.

questions.q: A migrating white blood cell travels 60 μm in 20 s. What is its average speed in m/s?
o: Multiplies distance by time instead of dividing (and mis-scales).
questions.x: The prefix micro (μ) means 10⁻⁶, so 60 μm = 6 × 10⁻⁵ m. Speed is distance ÷ time: 6 × 10⁻⁵ m ÷ 20 s = 3 × 10⁻⁶ m/s. Common prefixes: milli 10⁻³, micro 10⁻⁶, nano 10⁻⁹. Mixing them up shifts the answer by powers of 1000.

questions.q: A pendulum's period T depends only on its length L and g. Dimensional analysis requires T to be proportional to:
o: Correct: m ÷ (m/s²) = s², so √(L/g) has units of seconds.
Units are 1/s, a frequency, not a period.
Units are m²/s², which is not time.
questions.note: Check units of each candidate answer.
questions.x: Dimensional analysis: only one combination of L (m) and g (m/s²) gives seconds. L/g has units of s², so its square root has units of s. The full result is T = 2π√(L/g). √(g/L) has units of 1/s, which is a frequency, the inverse of a period.

questions.q: Forces of 3 N and 4 N act on an object at right angles to each other. What is the magnitude of their resultant?
o: Adds magnitudes as if the forces were parallel.
Subtracts magnitudes as if the forces were opposite.
Multiplies the magnitudes; vectors don't combine that way.
questions.x: Perpendicular vectors form the legs of a right triangle, and the resultant is the hypotenuse: √(3² + 4²) = 5 N. You simply add magnitudes (7 N) only when the vectors point the same way. Watch for 3-4-5 and 5-12-13 triangles on the MCAT.

questions.q: Two forces of 6 N and 10 N act on the same point in unknown directions. Which resultant magnitude is impossible?
o: Possible when the forces point in opposite directions.
Correct: the resultant must lie between 10 − 6 = 4 N and 10 + 6 = 16 N.
Possible when the forces point in the same direction.
Possible at an intermediate angle between the forces.
questions.note: Resultant range: |A − B| to A + B.
questions.x: Two vectors combine to a magnitude between their difference (opposite directions) and their sum (same direction). For 6 N and 10 N, that range is 4 N to 16 N, and any angle in between gives a value inside it. 17 N is larger than the maximum possible sum, so it is impossible.

questions.q: A 20 N force is applied at 30° above the horizontal. What is its horizontal component?
o: Uses sin 30°, which gives the vertical component.
Divides by cos 30°; a component can't exceed the full vector.
questions.x: The component next to the angle uses cosine: Fₓ = F cos θ = 20 × 0.87 ≈ 17 N. The vertical component is F sin θ = 10 N. A component can never be larger than the vector itself, so any answer above 20 N is ruled out right away.

questions.q: A hiker walks 4 km north, then 3 km west, then 4 km south. What is the magnitude of her displacement?
o: That is total distance traveled, a scalar.
Uses only the first two legs as a 3-4-5 triangle.
Adds only the north and west legs.
Correct: north and south legs cancel, leaving 3 km west.
questions.note: Displacement depends only on start and end points.
questions.x: Displacement is a vector from the start point to the end point. The 4 km north and 4 km south legs cancel, leaving 3 km west. Distance is a scalar that adds every leg (11 km), so it is always at least as large as the displacement magnitude.

questions.q: What is the magnitude of the cross product of two parallel vectors?
o: That is the cross product for perpendicular vectors.
Cross products multiply magnitudes; they never add them.
Correct: |A × B| = AB sin θ, and sin 0° = 0.
The product of their magnitudes times cos θ
That is the dot product, not the cross product.
questions.x: |A × B| = AB sin θ, so it is largest for perpendicular vectors and zero for parallel ones. The dot product does the reverse: A·B = AB cos θ is largest when the vectors are parallel. That is why torque (r × F) is zero when a force acts along the lever arm.

questions.q: A vector has components x = −5 and y = +5. What angle does it make with the positive x-axis (measured counterclockwise)?
o: Ignores the negative x-component (that would be quadrant I).
That is quadrant III, where both components are negative.
That is quadrant IV, where x is positive and y negative.
Correct: equal magnitudes give 45°, and (−,+) places it in quadrant II: 180° − 45°.
questions.x: The ratio |y/x| = 1 gives a reference angle of 45°. Then use the signs to pick the quadrant: x negative and y positive puts the vector in quadrant II, so the angle is 180° − 45° = 135°. Taking the arctangent without checking the signs gives the wrong quadrant.

questions.q: Vector A is 3 m east and vector B is 4 m north. What is A − B?
o: That is A + B; subtracting B reverses its direction.
Correct: A − B = A + (−B) = 3 m east + 4 m south; magnitude 5 m.
Subtracts magnitudes, which only works for parallel vectors.
Adds magnitudes instead of combining perpendicular components.
questions.note: Subtracting a vector = adding its reverse.
questions.x: To subtract a vector, add its reverse: A − B = A + (−B). Here that is 3 m east plus 4 m south. The legs are perpendicular, so the magnitude is 5 m, pointing south of east. A + B has the same magnitude but points north of east, so the direction is what tells them apart.

questions.q: A swimmer heads straight across a river at 1.5 m/s relative to the water, while the current flows at 2 m/s. What is her speed relative to the shore?
o: Adds the velocities as if they were parallel.
Subtracts them as if the current opposed her.
Correct: perpendicular velocities combine as √(1.5² + 2²) = 2.5 m/s.
Ignores the current's contribution to ground velocity.
questions.x: The ground velocity is the vector sum of the swimmer's velocity relative to the water and the water's velocity. These two are perpendicular, so they combine by Pythagoras: √(1.5² + 2²) = 2.5 m/s. You add or subtract them directly only if they are parallel or antiparallel.

questions.q: An object moves with constant velocity. Which quantity must be zero?
o: Correct: acceleration is the rate of change of velocity, which here is unchanging.
Constant velocity can be any nonzero speed.
Momentum is mv, nonzero for a moving mass.
questions.x: Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity. If velocity (both speed and direction) stays constant, acceleration must be zero, and by Newton's first law so must the net force. Speed and momentum can be any constant nonzero value.

questions.q: A car accelerates uniformly from 10 m/s to 30 m/s in 5 s. How far does it travel during this time?
o: Uses the final speed for the whole interval.
Correct: average velocity (10 + 30)/2 = 20 m/s, times 5 s = 100 m.
Uses the initial speed for the whole interval.
questions.note: Uniform acceleration: average velocity = (vᵢ + v_f)/2.
questions.x: With uniform acceleration, the average velocity is the mean of the initial and final velocities: (10 + 30)/2 = 20 m/s. Distance = average velocity × time = 100 m. You can check this with d = v₀t + ½at², using a = 4 m/s²: 50 + 50 = 100 m.

questions.q: A ball is thrown straight up at 20 m/s. How high does it rise (g = 10 m/s²)?
o: Forgets the factor of 2 in v² = 2gh.
Divides speed by g, which gives a time (in s), not a height.
questions.x: At the peak the velocity is zero, so v₀² = 2gh and h = v₀²/(2g) = 400/20 = 20 m. Energy gives the same result: ½mv² = mgh. Dividing v by g gives the time to the top (2 s), not the height.

questions.q: A ball is tossed straight up at 15 m/s and caught at the same height. How long is it in the air (g = 10 m/s²)?
o: That is only the time to reach the peak.
Adds an extra 1.5 s for no physical reason.
Correct: 1.5 s to stop at the top and 1.5 s to fall back.
questions.note: Up and down times are equal without air resistance.
questions.x: Gravity slows the ball by 10 m/s each second, so it reaches the top in 15/10 = 1.5 s. Without air resistance, the trip down is the mirror image of the trip up, so the total time is 2 × 1.5 = 3.0 s. A common mistake is to stop at the time to the peak.

questions.q: At the highest point of a ball's vertical toss, which statement is true (no air resistance)?
o: Velocity is zero; acceleration is 10 m/s² downward
Correct: the ball momentarily stops, but gravity still acts.
Velocity and acceleration are both zero
Gravity doesn't switch off; acceleration stays g.
Velocity is zero; acceleration is upward
Velocity is maximum; acceleration is zero
Speed is minimum (zero) at the top.
questions.note: Trap: v = 0 does not mean a = 0.
questions.x: Acceleration depends on the net force, not on velocity. Gravity acts the whole time, so acceleration stays 10 m/s² downward even at the top, where the velocity is zero for an instant. If acceleration were also zero there, the ball would just hover.

questions.q: On a velocity versus time graph, what represents an object's displacement?
o: The y-intercept is the initial velocity.
Correct: displacement is the integral of velocity over time.
That is the time when velocity is zero.
questions.x: The area under a v–t graph is velocity times time, which is displacement. Area below the axis counts as negative. The slope of a v–t graph is acceleration. Matching each graph feature to its units (m/s × s = m) keeps these straight.

questions.q: A position–time graph is a straight line sloping downward. What does this indicate?
o: Constant velocity in the negative direction
Correct: constant slope = constant velocity; negative slope = negative direction.
Acceleration would curve the x–t graph.
A straight line means speed is constant.
At rest would be a horizontal line.
questions.x: The slope of an x–t graph is velocity. A straight line has a constant slope, so the velocity is constant, and a downward slope means motion in the negative direction. Acceleration would make the x–t graph curve, so a straight line means zero acceleration.

questions.q: A car moving at 20 m/s brakes with a constant deceleration of 5 m/s². What is its stopping distance?
o: Forgets the factor of 2 in v² = 2ad.
Divides speed by deceleration, which gives a time.
Multiplies 20 m/s × 5 s (treating 5 as a time).
questions.x: When the final velocity is zero, v₀² = 2ad, so d = v₀²/(2a) = 400/10 = 40 m. Dividing v by a gives the stopping time (4 s), not the distance. As a check, the average speed of 10 m/s times 4 s = 40 m.

questions.q: A driver doubles her speed. With the same braking deceleration, her stopping distance changes by what factor?
o: Assumes distance is proportional to speed.
Uses a cubic dependence on speed.
Correct: d = v²/(2a), so doubling v quadruples d.
questions.note: Stopping distance scales with v².
questions.x: Stopping distance d = v²/(2a) depends on the square of speed. Doubling v therefore quadruples d (2² = 4). Equivalently, the car has 4 times the kinetic energy to get rid of with the same braking force. Assuming distance is simply proportional to speed is the trap.

questions.q: A runner starts from rest and accelerates at 2 m/s² for 4 s. How far does she travel?
o: Computes at = 8, which is the final speed in m/s, not the distance.
Uses t instead of t²: ½(2)(4) = 4.
questions.x: Starting from rest with constant acceleration, d = ½at² = ½(2)(4²) = 16 m. As a check, the speed rises to 8 m/s, so the average is 4 m/s, and 4 m/s × 4 s = 16 m. Forgetting the ½ gives twice the answer, and using t instead of t² gives the wrong scaling.

questions.q: An object is dropped from rest. What is the ratio of the distance it falls during the 2nd second to the distance during the 1st second?
o: Assumes distance per second grows linearly with time.
Compares total distance after 2 s (20 m) to the 1st second (5 m).
Correct: 5 m in the 1st second; 20 − 5 = 15 m in the 2nd; 15/5 = 3.
questions.note: Distances in successive seconds go 1 : 3 : 5 : 7.
questions.x: In free fall, distance grows as t², so the totals after 1 s and 2 s are 5 m and 20 m. The 2nd second covers 20 − 5 = 15 m, which is three times the 1st. In general, distances in successive equal intervals go in the odd-number ratio 1 : 3 : 5 : 7.

questions.q: A motion sensor records a cart's velocity as 2, 5, 8, and 11 m/s at t = 0, 1, 2, and 3 s. What is the cart's acceleration?
o: Correct: velocity rises 3 m/s every second.
Divides the final velocity by time, ignoring the initial 2 m/s.
That is the average velocity value, not an acceleration.
That is just the final velocity reading.
questions.x: Acceleration is the slope of velocity against time: (11 − 2) m/s ÷ 3 s = 3 m/s². The equal 3 m/s jumps each second show the acceleration is uniform. Dividing a single velocity reading by time ignores the initial velocity.

questions.q: A car travels 60 km at 30 km/h and then another 60 km at 60 km/h. What is its average speed for the trip?
o: Averages the two speeds, ignoring that more time was spent at 30 km/h.
Weights the faster leg too heavily.
questions.note: Average speed = total distance ÷ total time.
questions.x: Average speed is total distance ÷ total time, not the average of the two speeds. The slow leg takes 2 h and the fast leg 1 h, so 120 km ÷ 3 h = 40 km/h. Because the car spends more time going slowly, the answer is below 45 km/h, the simple mean.

questions.q: On a position versus time graph, what gives an object's instantaneous velocity?
o: Area under x–t has no standard kinematic meaning.
The y-value is position, not velocity.
The slope of the tangent line at that time
Correct: velocity is the derivative of position.
questions.x: Velocity is the derivative of position, so the instantaneous velocity is the slope of the tangent line at that moment. The height of the curve gives position. How quickly the slope changes (the curvature) reflects acceleration.

questions.q: During ventricular ejection, blood in the aorta accelerates from rest to 0.9 m/s in 0.1 s. What is its average acceleration?
o: Multiplies Δv by Δt instead of dividing.
Off by a factor of 10 in the division.
Gives the change in velocity, not the rate.
questions.x: Average acceleration is the change in velocity divided by the time interval: 0.9 m/s ÷ 0.1 s = 9 m/s², close to g. Dividing by 0.1 is the same as multiplying by 10. Giving Δv alone leaves out the time part of the rate.

questions.q: A ball is thrown straight down at 10 m/s from a 15 m ledge. What is its speed just before hitting the ground (g = 10 m/s²)?
o: Ignores the initial 10 m/s (that is a drop from rest).
Adds the 10 m/s initial speed to the 15 m height as if they were like quantities.
Adds initial speed linearly to a 20 m/s free-fall speed.
questions.note: Speeds add in quadrature in v² = v₀² + 2ad, not linearly.
questions.x: Use v² = v₀² + 2ad: 100 + 2(10)(15) = 400, so v = 20 m/s. Energy gives the same result. Speeds combine through their squares, so you cannot just add 10 m/s to the speed of a drop from rest (√300 ≈ 17 m/s).

questions.q: A student plots distance fallen versus time² for a dropped object and gets a straight line with slope 4.9 m/s². What value of g does this give?
o: Correct: d = ½gt², so slope = g/2 and g = 2 × 4.9.
Forgets that the slope is g/2, not g.
Halves the slope instead of doubling it.
questions.x: Starting from rest, d = ½gt². Plotting d against t² gives a straight line with slope g/2. So g = 2 × 4.9 = 9.8 m/s². To linearize data, compare the plot with y = mx and work out what the slope stands for.

questions.q: A researcher measures the stopping distance d of a cart at several initial speeds v under constant deceleration. Which plot should be linear?
o: d vs v would be a parabola.
d increases with v, not with 1/v.
The dependence is quadratic, not square-root.
Correct: d = v²/(2a), so d is proportional to v².
questions.note: Linearize by plotting against the variable as it appears in the equation.
questions.x: With constant deceleration, d = v²/(2a), so d is proportional to v². A plot of d against v² is a straight line through the origin with slope 1/(2a). A plot of d against v curves upward, which tells you the relationship is not linear.

questions.q: A sprinter's velocity rises linearly from 0 to 10 m/s over the first 4 s, then stays constant. How far does she run in the first 6 s?
o: Treats the whole 6 s as being at 10 m/s.
Uses an average speed of 5 m/s for all 6 s.
Correct: ½(4)(10) = 20 m, plus 10 m/s × 2 s = 20 m.
questions.note: Distance = area under v–t.
questions.x: Distance is the area under the v–t graph. The 0–4 s ramp is a triangle, ½(4)(10) = 20 m. The 4–6 s part is a rectangle, 10 × 2 = 20 m, so the total is 40 m. Using a single average speed for the whole run ignores that the speed stays at 10 m/s after 4 s.

questions.q: In a vacuum tube, a feather and a coin are dropped from rest through 1.25 m. What fall times are expected (g = 10 m/s²)?
o: Correct: 1.25 = ½(10)t², t = 0.5 s, independent of mass.
The coin takes less time than the feather
Without air resistance, mass doesn't affect free fall.
Solves 1.25 = 5t as if linear in t.
Divides height by g, which isn't a time.
questions.x: Without air, every object falls with the same acceleration g, whatever its mass. From d = ½gt², 1.25 = 5t², so t² = 0.25 and t = 0.5 s for both. On Earth the feather falls slower only because air drag is large compared with its tiny weight.

questions.q: For a projectile with no air resistance, which quantity stays constant throughout the flight?
o: Gravity changes vᵧ by 10 m/s every second.
Correct: no horizontal force acts, so vₓ is constant.
The path curves, so direction changes.
questions.x: In ideal projectile motion, the only force is gravity, which acts vertically. So the horizontal velocity never changes, while the vertical velocity changes by g each second. Speed and direction depend on vᵧ, so they change throughout the flight.

questions.q: A ball rolls off a 5 m high platform horizontally at 8 m/s. How far from the base does it land (g = 10 m/s²)?
o: Correct: fall time √(2h/g) = 1 s; 8 m/s × 1 s = 8 m.
Confuses horizontal range with the drop height.
questions.x: The horizontal and vertical motions are independent. Vertically, the ball falls 5 m from rest: t = √(2h/g) = √1 = 1 s. Horizontally, it keeps moving at 8 m/s during that time, so it lands 8 m from the base. The horizontal speed has no effect on the fall time.

questions.q: A projectile is launched at 20 m/s at 30° above the horizontal. How long does it take to reach maximum height?
o: That is the total flight time on level ground.
Correct: vᵧ = 20 sin 30° = 10 m/s; t = 10/10 = 1 s.
questions.x: Only the vertical component matters for the time to the peak: vᵧ = 20 sin 30° = 10 m/s. Gravity removes 10 m/s each second, so vᵧ reaches zero after 1 s. The horizontal component (≈17 m/s) affects range, not timing.

questions.q: A ball is kicked at 20 m/s at 30° above level ground. Approximately how far away does it land?
o: Correct: flight time 2 s; vₓ = 20 cos 30° ≈ 17.3 m/s; 17.3 × 2 ≈ 35 m.
Multiplies the vertical component (10 m/s) by the flight time.
Uses the full 20 m/s as the horizontal speed.
Uses only the time to reach the peak (1 s).
questions.x: The vertical component (10 m/s) sets the flight time: 1 s up and 1 s down, so 2 s in total. The horizontal component, 20 cos 30° ≈ 17.3 m/s, sets the distance: 17.3 × 2 ≈ 35 m. Using the full launch speed as the horizontal speed overestimates the range.

questions.q: On level ground, a projectile launched at 30° lands at the same spot as one launched at the same speed at:
o: 45° gives the maximum range, which is longer.
Correct: complementary angles give equal range because sin 2θ is the same.
At 15°, sin 2θ = sin 30° = 0.5, less than sin 60°, so the range is shorter.
A vertical launch has zero range.
questions.note: R = v² sin 2θ / g.
questions.x: On level ground, R = v² sin 2θ/g. Since sin 2θ = sin(180° − 2θ), angles that add to 90° give the same range: 30° and 60° both give sin 2θ = 0.87. The 60° shot goes higher and stays up longer but moves slower horizontally. 45° gives the maximum range.

questions.q: A projectile is launched at speed v and angle θ above horizontal. What is its speed at the top of its trajectory?
o: Correct: vᵧ = 0 at the peak; only the constant horizontal component remains.
Only the vertical component is zero at the top.
That is the initial vertical component, which is zero at the peak.
Speed decreases on the way up.
questions.x: At the peak the vertical velocity is zero, but the horizontal velocity, v cos θ, never changed. So the speed at the top is v cos θ, the minimum speed of the flight. It is zero only for a straight-up launch (θ = 90°).

questions.q: A ball is launched at 10 m/s at 45° above horizontal. What is its maximum height (g = 10 m/s²)?
o: Uses vᵧ (≈ 7.1 m/s) as if it were a height.
questions.x: Only the vertical component sets the height: vᵧ = 10 sin 45° ≈ 7.07 m/s, so vᵧ² = 50 m²/s². Then h = vᵧ²/(2g) = 50/20 = 2.5 m. Using the full 10 m/s gives 5 m, which is the height you would get by launching straight up.

questions.q: A crate is released from a plane flying horizontally at constant velocity. Ignoring air resistance, where is the crate relative to the plane as it falls?
o: That would require a horizontal force slowing the crate (air drag).
It depends on the crate's mass
Free-fall motion is independent of mass.
Correct: the crate keeps the plane's horizontal velocity.
questions.x: When released, the crate already has the plane's horizontal velocity. With no air resistance, no horizontal force acts, so that velocity stays the same. The crate stays directly below the plane while it falls. Only gravity, acting vertically, changes its motion.

questions.q: Students roll a ball horizontally off tables of different heights at the same speed. Quadrupling the height changes the horizontal range by what factor?
o: Assumes range is proportional to height.
Correct: fall time ∝ √h, so 4× height doubles time and range.
questions.x: The horizontal range is horizontal speed × fall time, and the fall time is t = √(2h/g). Since t ∝ √h, quadrupling the height doubles the fall time, which doubles the range. Assuming range is proportional to height ignores the square root.

questions.q: Compared with the ideal (no-drag) case, how does air resistance affect the launch angle that gives maximum range on level ground?
o: Higher arcs spend more time in the air and lose more to drag.
A vertical launch has zero range.
Correct: drag punishes long, high flights, favoring a lower trajectory.
questions.x: Without drag, the range is greatest at 45°. Drag removes energy the whole time the ball is moving, so high, long flights lose the most. A lower, faster trajectory spends less time in the air, so the best angle falls below 45°. That is why real-world throws and kicks often peak around 35–40°.

questions.q: One ball is dropped from a balcony while another is thrown horizontally at 5 m/s from the same height at the same instant. Which lands first?
o: Horizontal motion doesn't lengthen the fall.
They land at the same time
Correct: both start with zero vertical velocity and have the same vertical acceleration.
Horizontal speed doesn't speed up the fall.
Free fall is independent of mass.
questions.note: Horizontal and vertical motions are independent.
questions.x: Vertical motion does not depend on horizontal motion. Both balls start with zero vertical velocity, have the same downward acceleration g and fall the same height. So they hit the ground at the same moment. The thrown ball simply lands farther away.

questions.q: According to Newton's first law, an object experiencing zero net force will:
o: Keep moving at constant velocity, which may be zero
Correct: no net force means no change in velocity.
Slowing requires a net force such as friction.
Accelerate in its direction of motion
Circular motion requires a net centripetal force.
questions.note: Motion does not require force; changes in motion do.
questions.x: Newton's first law says velocity changes only when a net force acts. With zero net force, an object at rest stays at rest and a moving object keeps the same speed and direction. Everyday objects slow down because friction or drag is a real net force, not because motion naturally fades.

questions.q: A net force of 20 N acts on a 5 kg box. What is its acceleration?
questions.x: Newton's second law gives a = F_net/m = 20 N ÷ 5 kg = 4 m/s². A larger mass resists acceleration more, so mass goes in the denominator. Checking units confirms it: N/kg = (kg·m/s²)/kg = m/s².

questions.q: A horse pulls a cart, and by Newton's third law the cart pulls back on the horse with an equal force. Why can the horse and cart still accelerate forward?
o: The horse pulls slightly harder than the cart pulls back
Third-law forces are always exactly equal.
The paired forces act on different objects, and the ground pushes the horse forward
Correct: third-law pairs never cancel on one body; ground friction on the hooves drives the system.
Third-law forces cancel only when objects are at rest
Third-law pairs are equal and opposite in all cases.
The cart's reaction force is delayed by its inertia
questions.note: Trap: action–reaction forces act on different objects.
questions.x: Third-law pairs are equal and opposite, but they act on different objects, so they never cancel each other. Whether the horse moves depends on the net force on the horse alone: the ground's forward friction on its hooves is larger than the cart's backward pull. Thinking the horse pulls 'harder' is the classic misconception.

questions.q: A 60 kg person stands on a scale in an elevator accelerating upward at 2 m/s². What does the scale read (g = 10 m/s²)?
o: That is the reading at rest or constant velocity.
Uses g − a, which applies to downward acceleration.
Gives only the net force, ma.
questions.x: A scale reads the normal force. For upward acceleration, N − mg = ma, so N = m(g + a) = 60 × 12 = 720 N. The scale reads more than her true weight because the floor must both hold her up and accelerate her upward. Downward acceleration would make the reading smaller.

questions.q: A 70 kg person rides an elevator moving downward at a constant 3 m/s. What does a scale under her read (g = 10 m/s²)?
o: Treats downward motion as downward acceleration.
Adds 3 m/s as if it were an acceleration.
Correct: constant velocity means zero acceleration, so N = mg.
questions.note: Scale readings depend on acceleration, not velocity.
questions.x: The scale reading depends on acceleration, not on velocity. At constant velocity, in any direction, a = 0, so N = mg = 700 N. Moving downward feels lighter only while the elevator is speeding up downward or slowing down on the way up.

questions.q: An elevator cable snaps and the car falls freely. What does a scale under a passenger read?
o: That would be upward acceleration of g.
That would be downward acceleration of g/2.
Correct: passenger and scale accelerate together at g, so no normal force is needed.
questions.x: In free fall, the passenger and the scale both accelerate at g, so the scale does not need to push on her: N = m(g − g) = 0. Gravity still acts on her fully. Apparent weightlessness means zero normal force, not zero gravity.

questions.q: On a frictionless surface, a 10 N horizontal force pushes a 2 kg block, which pushes a 3 kg block in front of it. What force does the 2 kg block exert on the 3 kg block?
o: Ignores that part of the applied force accelerates the 2 kg block.
That is the net force on the 2 kg block.
Correct: a = 10/5 = 2 m/s²; force on the 3 kg block = 3 × 2 = 6 N.
Splits the force equally regardless of mass.
questions.x: First find the acceleration of the whole system: 10 N ÷ 5 kg = 2 m/s². The only horizontal force on the 3 kg block is the push from the 2 kg block, so it must equal 3 × 2 = 6 N. The remaining 4 N accelerates the 2 kg block. The applied force is not passed on in full.

questions.q: Masses of 3 kg and 5 kg hang on opposite sides of a frictionless, massless pulley. What is their acceleration (g = 10 m/s²)?
o: Divides the 20 N weight difference by the heavier mass only, not the total mass.
Uses the heavier weight (50 N) instead of the difference.
Treats the heavier mass as if in free fall.
questions.note: Atwood: a = (m₂ − m₁)g/(m₁ + m₂).
questions.x: Treat both masses as one system. The net driving force is the difference in weights, (5 − 3) × 10 = 20 N, and it accelerates the total mass of 8 kg: a = 2.5 m/s². Dividing by only one mass forgets that both masses move together.

questions.q: Masses of 2 kg and 6 kg hang over a frictionless, massless pulley. What is the string tension (g = 10 m/s²)?
o: That is the 2 kg weight; tension must exceed it to accelerate that mass up.
That is the 6 kg weight; tension must be less to let it accelerate down.
Averages the two weights instead of applying F = ma.
questions.x: First, a = (6 − 2)(10)/8 = 5 m/s². For the 2 kg mass accelerating upward, T − 20 = 2 × 5, so T = 30 N. The answer must lie between the two weights: above 20 N to lift the lighter mass and below 60 N so the heavier one can fall.

questions.q: An astronaut travels to the Moon, where g is about 1/6 of Earth's. How do her mass and weight compare to their Earth values?
o: Correct: mass is intrinsic; weight = mg.
questions.x: Mass measures how much matter an object has and how much it resists acceleration. It is the same everywhere. Weight is the gravitational force, W = mg, so it changes with local g. On the Moon, her mass is the same and her weight is about 1/6 of its Earth value.

questions.q: A 1000 kg car slows uniformly from 20 m/s to rest in 4 s. What is the magnitude of the average braking force?
o: Multiplies mass by speed (that is momentum, in kg·m/s).
questions.x: The deceleration is Δv/Δt = 20/4 = 5 m/s², so F = ma = 1000 × 5 = 5000 N. Impulse gives the same result: F = Δp/Δt = 20,000 kg·m/s ÷ 4 s. Multiplying mass by speed alone gives momentum, not force.

questions.q: A book rests on a table. What is the Newton's third-law partner of Earth's gravitational pull on the book?
o: The book's gravitational pull on Earth
Correct: third-law pairs are the same type of force between the same two objects.
The table's normal force on the book
Equal and opposite here, but it's a different force type acting on the same object.
The book's push on the table
That is the partner of the normal force.
That involves Earth and the table, not the book.
questions.note: Third-law pairs: same interaction, two different objects.
questions.x: A third-law pair is two sides of one interaction: if A pulls on B, B pulls on A with the same type of force. Earth pulls the book gravitationally, so the book pulls Earth gravitationally. The normal force is equal and opposite here, but it acts on the same object and is a different force, so it is not the pair.

questions.q: A rope lifts a 10 kg crate vertically with a tension of 150 N. What is the crate's acceleration (g = 10 m/s²)?
o: Correct: net force = 150 − 100 = 50 N; a = 50/10 = 5 m/s².
questions.x: Add up the forces on the crate: tension up (150 N) and weight down (100 N), so the net force is 50 N upward. Then a = 50/10 = 5 m/s² upward. Leaving out the weight treats tension as the net force, which is a common free-body mistake.

questions.q: Students apply the same net force to carts of different mass and plot acceleration versus 1/m. What should the graph look like?
o: That is a versus m, not a versus 1/m.
Acceleration does change with mass at fixed force.
The slope is F, since a = F × (1/m).
A straight line through the origin with slope equal to F
Correct: a = F(1/m), a direct proportion with slope F.
questions.x: With F held constant, a = F × (1/m). This has the form y = mx, with 1/m on the x-axis and slope F. So a plot of a against 1/m is a straight line through the origin. A plot of a against m would instead be a curve that falls toward zero.

questions.q: A skydiver falls at terminal velocity. What is the net force on her?
o: That would be free fall with no drag.
Drag exceeds weight only while slowing, e.g., after the parachute opens.
At terminal velocity there is no acceleration.
Correct: drag equals weight, so velocity is constant.
questions.x: At terminal velocity, drag has grown until it equals her weight. The net force is zero, so the acceleration is zero and the speed stays constant. Drag exceeds weight only briefly, for example right after a parachute opens, when she is slowing down.

questions.q: A 60 kg person pushes off the ground in a vertical jump with an average ground force of 1500 N. What is her upward acceleration during push-off (g = 10 m/s²)?
o: Correct: net force = 1500 − 600 = 900 N; a = 900/60 = 15 m/s².
Adds her weight to the ground force.
questions.x: Her weight is 600 N, so the net upward force during push-off is 1500 − 600 = 900 N, and a = 900/60 = 15 m/s². The ground must push harder than her weight to give her upward acceleration. Using the full 1500 N as the net force forgets gravity.

questions.q: A passenger's car is struck from behind. Why does the passenger's head seem to snap backward?
o: The collision pushes the head backward
No backward force acts on the head; the car is pushed forward.
The head is pulled backward by gravity
The seat accelerates the torso forward while the head's inertia keeps it in place
Correct: Newton's first law; the head lags until the neck pulls it.
The motion is passive inertia, not a reflex.
questions.x: In a rear-end collision, the seat pushes the torso forward. The head has no force on it at first, so by inertia it stays where it was. Relative to the car, it looks like the head snaps backward until the neck pulls it along. Nothing pushes the head backward.

questions.q: For most pairs of surfaces, how does the coefficient of kinetic friction compare with the coefficient of static friction?
o: Correct: it takes more force to start sliding than to keep sliding.
μk depends on speed while μs is always zero
Static friction is not zero; it resists the onset of sliding.
questions.x: Static friction can grow up to μsN to stop sliding from starting. Once the surfaces slide, the microscopic contacts have less time to bond, so kinetic friction is usually smaller (μk < μs). That is why something stuck needs a big push to start and less to keep it moving.

questions.q: A 20 kg box rests on a floor with μs = 0.5 and μk = 0.3. What minimum horizontal force will start it moving (g = 10 m/s²)?
o: Uses μk, which applies once the box is already sliding.
Correct: maximum static friction = μsmg = 0.5 × 200 = 100 N.
Adds the static and kinetic friction values.
questions.x: To start the box moving, the push must beat the maximum static friction, μsN = 0.5 × 200 = 100 N. Kinetic friction (60 N) matters only after it is already sliding. That difference is why a box seems to suddenly give way once it starts moving.

questions.q: A 50 kg crate is pushed horizontally at constant speed across a floor with μk = 0.2. What push is required (g = 10 m/s²)?
o: Constant velocity means zero net force, not zero applied force when friction acts.
Correct: constant speed means push = kinetic friction = 0.2 × 500 N.
questions.x: Constant speed means zero net force, so the push must exactly balance kinetic friction. Here f = μkmg = 0.2 × 500 = 100 N. Zero net force does not mean zero applied force; it means the forces cancel.

questions.q: A 10 kg box sits on a floor with μs = 0.4. A 25 N horizontal push does not move it. What is the static friction force (g = 10 m/s²)?
o: That is the maximum possible static friction, not the actual value.
Friction must oppose the push for the box to stay at rest.
Correct: static friction matches the applied force up to its maximum (40 N).
Subtracts push from the maximum; friction simply balances the push.
questions.note: Trap: μsN is a ceiling, not the value.
questions.x: Static friction is only as large as it needs to be to stop sliding, up to the limit μsN (40 N here). A 25 N push is below that limit, so friction is exactly 25 N in the opposite direction and the box stays still. Plugging in μsN when the box is not about to slip is the trap.

questions.q: A box slides across a floor with μk = 0.25 at an initial speed of 5 m/s. How far does it slide before stopping (g = 10 m/s²)?
o: Correct: a = μkg = 2.5 m/s²; d = v²/(2a) = 25/5 = 5 m.
Forgets the factor of 2 in v² = 2ad.
Uses the deceleration value as the distance.
Uses a = 0.25 m/s², forgetting to multiply μk by g.
questions.x: Kinetic friction is the only horizontal force, so the deceleration is a = μkg = 0.25 × 10 = 2.5 m/s², and mass cancels. Then d = v²/(2a) = 25/5 = 5 m. Energy gives the same result: ½mv² = μkmgd.

questions.q: A brick slides on its broad face, then is turned onto its narrow edge on the same surface. How does the kinetic friction force change?
o: Correct: friction ≈ μN and is independent of apparent contact area.
It increases because pressure is greater
Higher pressure on a smaller area gives the same total force.
It decreases because the contact area is smaller
Contact area does not appear in f = μN.
questions.x: In the simple friction model, f = μN, so the force depends only on the normal force and the surfaces. Turning the brick changes the contact area but not its weight. The pressure is higher on a smaller area, and the total friction stays the same. Contact area does not appear in the equation.

questions.q: A sled is pulled with a rope angled 30° above horizontal rather than horizontally, with the same tension. Why does kinetic friction decrease?
o: Friction depends on the angle of the rope directly
μk is a property of the surfaces, not the rope.
The upward component of tension reduces the normal force
Correct: N = mg − T sin θ, and friction = μkN.
The horizontal component is actually smaller.
Mass is unchanged; only the normal force changes.
questions.x: Friction depends on the normal force. When the rope is angled, part of the tension pulls upward, so the floor supports less of the weight: N = mg − T sin θ. Less normal force means less friction, f = μkN. μk depends only on the surfaces and does not change.

questions.q: Synovial fluid gives a knee joint a friction coefficient of about 0.01. If the joint carries a 1000 N load, what is the friction force?
questions.x: Friction is f = μN = 0.01 × 1000 N = 10 N. Synovial fluid gives one of the lowest friction coefficients known, which keeps joint wear and heat low. The friction force is the coefficient times the load, never the load itself.

questions.q: Why do anti-lock brakes typically shorten a car's stopping distance?
o: They increase the normal force on the tires
ABS doesn't change the car's weight on the road.
They convert kinetic friction into rolling resistance
Rolling resistance is tiny and wouldn't stop the car faster.
They raise μk by heating the tires
ABS works by preventing lockup, not by heating.
They keep tires rolling, so static rather than kinetic friction acts
Correct: μs > μk, so the maximum braking force is larger.
questions.x: A wheel that is rolling without skidding grips the road with static friction. A locked, skidding wheel slides with kinetic friction. Because μs > μk, ABS keeps the wheels just short of locking, which lets the car brake with a larger maximum friction force. Steering control is also kept.

questions.q: A block rests on a board that is slowly tilted. It begins to slide when the angle reaches 37° (sin 37° = 0.6, cos 37° = 0.8). What is μs?
o: Uses sin θ instead of tan θ.
Uses cos θ instead of tan θ.
Uses the angle in degrees divided by 100.
Correct: at the slipping point μs = tan θ = 0.6/0.8.
questions.x: At the point of slipping, static friction is at its maximum: μsmg cos θ = mg sin θ, so μs = tan θ. Here tan 37° = 0.6/0.8 = 0.75. Mass and g cancel out, which is why a tilting-board experiment measures μs directly.

questions.q: A block slides down a frictionless 30° incline. What is its acceleration (g = 10 m/s²)?
o: Uses cos 30°, which belongs to the normal direction.
That is free fall, not motion along an incline.
A frictionless incline always produces acceleration.
questions.x: On a frictionless incline, only the component of gravity along the slope accelerates the block: a = g sin θ = 10 × 0.5 = 5 m/s². The g cos θ component points into the surface and is balanced by the normal force. Check the limits: θ = 90° gives free fall and θ = 0° gives no acceleration.

questions.q: A 10 kg block rests on a 30° incline. What is the normal force on it (g = 10 m/s²)?
o: Uses sin 30°, which gives the component along the incline.
That is the normal force on level ground.
Divides by cos 30° instead of multiplying.
questions.x: Perpendicular to the incline, the normal force balances the component of gravity pressing into the surface: N = mg cos θ = 100 × 0.87 ≈ 87 N. The mg sin θ component (50 N) points along the slope. As the incline gets steeper, N shrinks below the block's weight.

questions.q: A block slides down a 37° incline with μk = 0.5 (sin 37° = 0.6, cos 37° = 0.8). What is its acceleration (g = 10 m/s²)?
o: Correct: a = g(sin θ − μk cos θ) = 10(0.6 − 0.4).
Multiplies μk by sin θ instead of cos θ: 10(0.6 − 0.3).
questions.x: Along the slope, gravity pulls down with mg sin θ and friction pulls back with μkmg cos θ. So a = g(sin θ − μk cos θ) = 10(0.6 − 0.5 × 0.8) = 2 m/s². Friction depends on the normal force, which involves cos θ, not sin θ.

questions.q: The angle of a frictionless incline is increased. How do the block's acceleration and the normal force change?
o: N = mg cos θ falls as θ rises.
That is what happens when the angle decreases.
Acceleration increases; normal force is unchanged
Correct: a = g sin θ rises; N = mg cos θ falls.
questions.x: Making the incline steeper shifts gravity from pressing into the surface to pulling along it. The acceleration g sin θ grows, while the normal force mg cos θ shrinks. At 90°, the block would be in free fall with zero normal force.

questions.q: What force, directed along the incline, pushes a 20 kg box up a frictionless 30° incline at constant speed (g = 10 m/s²)?
o: That is the full weight, needed only for a vertical lift.
Correct: constant speed means F = mg sin 30° = 200 × 0.5.
Gravity's component along the incline must be balanced.
questions.x: Constant speed means zero net force along the incline. So the push must balance only the component of gravity along the slope: mg sin 30° = 200 × 0.5 = 100 N. The incline means you need less force than lifting the box straight up (200 N), but you push it a longer distance.

questions.q: Two identical blocks slide from rest down frictionless ramps of the same height, one steep and one shallow. Which statement is correct?
o: Both arrive at the same time with the same speed
The shallow ramp is longer and has smaller acceleration.
The steep-ramp block arrives first, and both have the same final speed
Correct: final speed = √(2gh) for both; the steep ramp has larger acceleration and shorter path.
The steep-ramp block arrives first with greater speed
Speed depends only on height drop.
It travels farther with less acceleration.
questions.x: With no friction, energy conservation gives v = √(2gh) at the bottom for any ramp of the same height. The steep ramp has a larger acceleration (g sin θ) and a shorter path, so its block arrives first. The final speed depends only on height, while the time depends on the ramp's shape.

questions.q: The mass of a block sliding down a frictionless incline is doubled. What happens to its acceleration?
o: Correct: a = g sin θ, independent of mass.
Doubled force acts on doubled mass.
No quantity here scales with mass squared.
questions.x: The gravitational pull along the slope, mg sin θ, grows with mass, but so does the inertia. So a = g sin θ, and mass cancels out. This is the same reason all objects fall with the same acceleration in a vacuum.

questions.q: A wheelchair ramp rises 1 m for every 12 m of horizontal run. Ignoring friction, about what force along the ramp is needed to push a 100 kg person and chair up at constant speed?
o: That is the full weight, needed only for a vertical lift.
Correct: sin θ ≈ 1/12 for a gentle slope; 1000 N × 1/12 ≈ 83 N.
Multiplies the weight by 12 instead of dividing.
Uses sin 30°; the ramp is far shallower.
questions.x: For gentle slopes, sin θ ≈ tan θ = rise/run = 1/12. The push needed at constant speed is mg sin θ ≈ 1000/12 ≈ 83 N. A shallow ramp trades force for distance: the work mgh is the same, but it is spread over a path about 12 times longer.

questions.q: An object moves in a circle at constant speed. In what direction does its acceleration point?
o: Along the velocity, tangent to the path
A tangential component would change the speed.
Centrifugal force is a fictitious force in the rotating frame.
Toward the center of the circle
Correct: centripetal acceleration changes the direction of velocity.
questions.x: In uniform circular motion, the speed stays the same but the direction keeps changing, so the velocity changes. The acceleration points toward the center (centripetal), perpendicular to the velocity, and has magnitude v²/r. Centrifugal force is not a real force; it appears only when you analyze from inside the rotating frame.

questions.q: A 0.5 kg ball on a 1 m string is whirled in a horizontal circle at 4 m/s. Ignoring gravity, what is the string tension?
o: Divides by 2r, as if the radius were 2 m.
questions.x: The tension is the only force pulling the ball toward the center, so it supplies the centripetal force: T = mv²/r = 0.5 × 16/1 = 8 N. Speed is squared, so forgetting to square it (2 N) is the main trap.

questions.q: At the same radius, the speed of an object in uniform circular motion is doubled. By what factor does the required centripetal force change?
o: Correct: F = mv²/r, so F ∝ v².
Force increases, not decreases, with speed.
The force depends strongly on speed.
questions.x: Centripetal force is F = mv²/r. Because speed is squared, doubling v requires 2² = 4 times the inward force. This is why taking a curve at twice the speed needs four times the grip from the tires.

questions.q: A centrifuge holds a sample 0.1 m from the axis moving at 30 m/s. What is the centripetal acceleration in multiples of g (g = 10 m/s²)?
o: Off by a factor of 10 in v²/r.
Uses v/r (300) instead of v²/r and never divides by g.
questions.x: Centripetal acceleration is a = v²/r = 900/0.1 = 9000 m/s². Dividing by g = 10 m/s² gives 900 g. Centrifuges separate particles because this huge effective gravity speeds up sedimentation.

questions.q: A car crosses the top of a circular hill of radius 40 m at 20 m/s. What is the normal force from the road on the car?
o: True only at very low speed or on level road.
That would be at the bottom of a dip, not the top of a hill.
Correct: v²/r = 400/40 = 10 m/s² = g, so gravity alone supplies the centripetal force.
questions.note: At a hilltop, N = m(g − v²/r).
questions.x: At the top of a hill, the net downward force must supply the centripetal force: mg − N = mv²/r. Here v²/r = 400/40 = 10 m/s² = g, so N = 0, and the car is just about to leave the road. A normal force that grows above the weight happens at the bottom of a dip, where N = m(g + v²/r).

questions.q: A ball whirled on a string moves in a horizontal circle. If the string snaps, what path does the ball initially follow (seen from above)?
o: A straight line tangent to the circle
Correct: with no centripetal force, it continues with its instantaneous velocity.
No outward force exists; that is the centrifugal misconception.
Circular motion needs a centripetal force.
With no horizontal force, the path is straight.
questions.x: Circular motion continues only while a centripetal force keeps bending the path. When the string snaps, that force is gone, and by Newton's first law the ball moves in a straight line along its velocity at that moment, which is tangent to the circle. There was never an outward force to throw it radially outward.

questions.q: What is the minimum speed a car needs at the top of a vertical loop of radius 10 m to stay on the track (g = 10 m/s²)?
o: A stopped car would fall off the top of the loop.
Correct: at minimum speed N = 0, so mg = mv²/r and v = √(gr) = 10 m/s.
Uses gr without the square root.
questions.x: At the top of the loop, gravity and the normal force both point toward the center: mg + N = mv²/r. The lowest speed is when the track just stops pushing (N = 0), so v = √(gr) = √100 = 10 m/s. Any slower and gravity pulls the car into a tighter curve than the track, so it falls away.

questions.q: A car rounds a flat curve of radius 50 m where μs = 0.5. What is the maximum speed without skidding (g = 10 m/s²)?
o: Correct: μsg = v²/r, so v = √(0.5 × 10 × 50) = √250 ≈ 16 m/s.
Uses μsr = 25 without the square root and without g.
questions.note: Max speed on a flat curve is independent of mass.
questions.x: On a flat curve, static friction provides the centripetal force, so the most it can supply is μsmg = mv²/r. Mass cancels: v_max = √(μsgr) = √250 ≈ 16 m/s. Static friction applies because the tires are not sliding sideways, and leaving out g or the square root gives the wrong units.

questions.q: At fixed radius 0.5 m, a student measures centripetal force versus v² for a rotating mass and finds a slope of 4 N·s²/m². What is the mass?
o: Divides the slope by r instead of multiplying.
Correct: F = (m/r)v², so slope = m/r and m = 4 × 0.5 = 2 kg.
Assumes the slope equals the mass.
Divides r by the slope (0.5/4) instead of multiplying them.
questions.x: With r fixed, F = (m/r)v², so a plot of F against v² is a straight line with slope m/r. So m = slope × r = 4 × 0.5 = 2 kg. When you linearize data, work out which combination of constants the slope stands for before solving.

questions.q: The distance between two masses doubles. What happens to the gravitational force between them?
questions.x: Gravity follows an inverse-square law: F = Gm₁m₂/r². Doubling the separation divides the force by 2² = 4. Assuming F ∝ 1/r gives one-half, which is the most common mistake.

questions.q: A planet has the same mass as Earth but twice its radius. What is the surface gravitational acceleration (Earth g = 10 m/s²)?
o: Correct: g ∝ M/R², so doubling R gives g/4.
Multiplies by R² instead of dividing.
questions.x: Surface gravity is g = GM/R². With the same mass and double the radius, g becomes 1/2² = 1/4 of Earth's, or 2.5 m/s². A larger radius puts the surface farther from the center of mass, which weakens gravity there.

questions.q: An astronaut on an orbiting space station feels weightless even though gravity there is about 90% of its surface value. Why?
o: Gravity is still about 90% of surface strength.
In an inertial frame, gravity is unbalanced; it supplies centripetal force.
She and the station are in continuous free fall together
Correct: everything accelerates at the same rate, so no normal force acts.
The station's mass shields her from Earth's gravity
questions.x: Gravity in low orbit is nearly as strong as at the surface. It supplies the centripetal force that keeps the station curving around Earth. She and the station fall at the same rate, so the floor does not push on her and she feels weightless. Weightlessness means zero normal force, not zero gravity.

questions.q: At what distance from Earth's center is the gravitational acceleration one-ninth of its surface value? (R = Earth's radius)
o: Takes the square root of 3 instead of 9.
Squares the factor instead of taking its root.
questions.x: g falls off as 1/r², measured from Earth's center. To get g/9 you need r² = 9R², so r = 3R, which is 2R above the surface. Using 9R treats gravity as though it fell off as 1/r.

questions.q: Two satellites, one of mass m and one of mass 2m, orbit Earth in circular orbits of the same radius. How do their orbital speeds compare?
o: Correct: GMm/r² = mv²/r gives v = √(GM/r), independent of satellite mass.
The heavier one is faster by √2
The heavier one is slower by √2
The heavier one is twice as fast
questions.x: Setting gravity equal to the centripetal force, GMm/r² = mv²/r, the satellite's mass cancels and v = √(GM/r). Orbital speed depends only on the planet's mass and the orbit's radius. This is the same reason a feather and a hammer fall together in a vacuum.

questions.q: A satellite's circular orbital radius is quadrupled. By what factor does its orbital speed change?
o: Correct: v = √(GM/r), so 4× radius gives 1/√4 = ½ the speed.
questions.x: Circular orbital speed is v = √(GM/r), so v ∝ 1/√r. Quadrupling the radius multiplies the speed by 1/√4 = ½. Higher orbits are slower, even though moving the satellite up to them takes energy.

questions.q: How does the gravitational force Earth exerts on the Moon compare with the force the Moon exerts on Earth?
o: Earth's force is about 81 times larger
Earth's mass is larger, but the force pair is equal.
The forces are equal and opposite.
Correct: they form a Newton's third-law pair.
Earth's force is larger by the ratio of their radii
Radii don't change the third-law equality.
questions.note: Equal forces, but the Moon's acceleration is far larger.
questions.x: The pull of Earth on the Moon and the pull of the Moon on Earth are a Newton's third-law pair, so they have exactly the same magnitude. The effects are different: a = F/m, so the Moon's much smaller mass gives it a much larger acceleration. The trap is thinking the larger mass pulls harder.

questions.q: A satellite moves from a lower circular orbit to a higher one. How does its gravitational potential energy (U = −GMm/r) change?
o: Moving away from Earth raises gravitational PE.
Correct: larger r makes −GMm/r closer to zero.
U = −GMm/r is negative for any finite r.
questions.x: U = −GMm/r is negative and gets closer to zero as r grows. So moving to a higher orbit increases the potential energy. Zero is the reference at infinite separation, and lifting a satellite against gravity always increases U, even though U stays negative.

questions.q: Which conditions must hold for an extended object to be in static equilibrium?
o: Net force and net torque are both zero, and it is at rest
Correct: translational and rotational equilibrium, with no motion.
Net force is zero; torque may be nonzero
Net torque is zero; force may be nonzero
Nonzero net force causes linear acceleration.
Forces can be nonzero as long as they balance.
questions.x: Static equilibrium needs zero net force (no linear acceleration), zero net torque (no angular acceleration), and the object at rest. The individual forces do not have to be zero; they only have to balance. Zero net force alone is not enough, because a couple of forces could still make the object rotate.

questions.q: A 30 kg child sits 2 m from a seesaw's pivot. How far from the pivot on the other side must a 40 kg child sit to balance?
o: Equal distances balance only equal masses.
Inverts the ratio; the heavier child must sit closer.
questions.x: For balance, the torques about the pivot must be equal: m₁g d₁ = m₂g d₂. So 30 × 2 = 40 × d, giving d = 1.5 m. The heavier child sits closer to the pivot, in inverse proportion to mass. Flipping the ratio puts the heavier child farther out, which would make that side go down.

questions.q: A 10 N force is applied to a door 0.4 m from the hinge, at 30° to the door's surface. What torque does it produce?
o: Treats the force as perpendicular to the door.
Only a force along the door (θ = 0°) gives zero torque.
questions.x: Torque is τ = rF sin θ, where θ is the angle between the lever arm (along the door) and the force. Here that is 0.4 × 10 × sin 30° = 2 N·m. Only the force component perpendicular to the door turns it. Using cos 30° picks the component along the door, which only pulls on the hinge.

questions.q: The lever arm (moment arm) of a force about an axis is defined as the:
o: Perpendicular distance from the axis to the force's line of action
Distance from the axis to the object's center of mass
That locates weight's lever arm only in special cases.
Distance along the force's line of action
Distance along the line of action contributes no torque.
questions.x: The lever arm is the perpendicular distance from the rotation axis to the line along which the force acts, so τ = F × lever arm. Sliding a force along its own line does not change the torque. The center of mass matters only for the weight's lever arm, not for every force.

questions.q: The biceps inserts 4 cm from the elbow. With the forearm horizontal, a hand holds a 50 N weight 32 cm from the elbow. Ignoring the forearm's weight, what biceps force is needed?
questions.note: The forearm is a third-class lever: big muscle force, small load.
questions.x: Take torques about the elbow: F_biceps × 4 cm = 50 N × 32 cm, so F = 400 N. The biceps attaches close to the pivot, so it needs a force many times larger than the load. In exchange, a small muscle shortening produces a large, fast movement of the hand, which is the trade-off of a third-class lever.

questions.q: A uniform 4 m beam weighing 200 N rests on supports at each end. A 400 N person stands 1 m from the left end. What force does the left support exert?
o: That is the right support's force.
Correct: torques about the right end: L(4) = 200(2) + 400(3), so L = 400 N.
That is the total load on both supports.
questions.x: Taking torques about the right support removes that unknown. The beam's weight acts at its center, 2 m from the right end, and the person is 3 m away: L × 4 = 200 × 2 + 400 × 3, so L = 400 N. As a check, the forces must add to 600 N, so R = 200 N. The person stands nearer the left, so that support carries more.

questions.q: A uniform meter stick balances at its 50 cm mark. A 100 g mass hangs at the 20 cm mark. Where must a 150 g mass hang to restore balance?
o: Uses the same 30 cm lever arm as the lighter mass.
Correct: 100 × 30 = 150 × d gives d = 20 cm right of center.
Uses the inverted ratio, 45 cm from center.
Places it on the same side as the 100 g mass.
questions.x: Use torques about the 50 cm pivot. The 100 g mass is 30 cm left, so 100 × 30 = 150 × d and d = 20 cm, which is the 70 cm mark. The heavier mass sits closer to the pivot. The stick's own weight acts at the pivot, so it adds no torque.

questions.q: A 4 kg lamp hangs from two strings, each making 60° with the horizontal ceiling. What is the tension in each string (g = 10 m/s²)?
o: Splits the weight equally, ignoring the angle.
Assigns the full weight to each string.
Correct: 2T sin 60° = 40 N, so T = 40/1.73 ≈ 23 N.
Divides by sin 60° without splitting between strings.
questions.x: Each string pulls upward with T sin 60°, and together they must hold up the 40 N weight: 2T sin 60° = 40, so T ≈ 23 N. Each tension is more than half the weight, because part of each pull is horizontal and cancels the other string's horizontal pull. Shallower strings would need even more tension.

questions.q: A 2 kg mass sits at x = 0 and a 6 kg mass at x = 4 m. Where is their center of mass?
o: Takes the midpoint, ignoring the masses.
Places it at the heavier mass.
questions.x: The center of mass is the mass-weighted average position: (2 × 0 + 6 × 4)/(2 + 6) = 3 m. It always lies between the masses and closer to the heavier one. The geometric midpoint (2 m) is correct only when the masses are equal.

questions.q: Why does a person carrying a heavy backpack lean forward?
o: To increase friction with the ground
Weight is mg regardless of posture.
To shorten the backpack's moment of inertia
Static balance depends on the center of mass, not inertia.
To keep the combined center of mass over the feet
Correct: stability requires the center of mass above the base of support.
questions.x: A standing person is stable only while the combined center of mass stays above the base of support (the feet). A backpack shifts the center of mass backward. Leaning forward moves it back over the feet so that gravity produces no tipping torque.

questions.q: Model the foot as a lever pivoting at the ankle. On tiptoe on one foot, a 600 N upward floor force acts 15 cm in front of the ankle, and the Achilles tendon attaches 5 cm behind it. What is the tendon tension?
o: Adds the floor force to the tendon tension.
questions.x: Taking torques about the ankle, the tendon's pull (5 cm behind) must balance the floor force (15 cm in front): T × 5 = 600 × 15, so T = 1800 N. The short tendon lever arm means the tendon must pull three times the body weight. This is why the Achilles tendon carries such large loads.

questions.q: How much work is done lifting a 2 kg box 3 m straight up at constant speed (g = 10 m/s²)?
o: Halves the work as if using ½mgh.
questions.x: At constant speed, the lifting force equals the weight, mg = 20 N, so the work is W = Fd = 20 × 3 = 60 J. This equals the gain in gravitational potential energy, mgh. The kinetic energy does not change, so none of the work goes into speed.

questions.q: A sled is pulled 10 m by a 50 N force directed 60° above the horizontal. How much work does this force do?
o: Only a force perpendicular to motion does zero work.
questions.x: Only the force component along the displacement does work: W = Fd cos θ = 50 × 10 × cos 60° = 250 J. The vertical component, F sin θ, is perpendicular to the motion and does no work. Using sin 60° picks out that vertical component by mistake.

questions.q: A ball is thrown straight up and caught at the same height. What net work does gravity do over the whole trip?
o: That is only the downward half.
Correct: negative work on the way up cancels positive work on the way down.
That is only the upward half.
The two halves have opposite signs.
questions.note: Gravity is conservative: zero work around a closed path.
questions.x: On the way up, gravity opposes the motion and does −mgh of work. On the way down, it does +mgh. Over the closed path the total is zero, as for any conservative force. Gravity's work depends only on the start and end heights, and here they are the same.

questions.q: A 5 kg box slides 4 m across a floor with μk = 0.2. How much work does friction do on the box (g = 10 m/s²)?
o: Correct: f = 0.2 × 50 = 10 N, opposite motion; W = −10 × 4.
Friction opposes motion, so its work is negative.
Uses weight (50 N) instead of friction force.
Uses mass instead of weight for the normal force.
questions.x: Kinetic friction is f = μkmg = 0.2 × 50 = 10 N, pointing opposite the motion. So its work is W = −fd = −10 × 4 = −40 J. Friction takes mechanical energy away and turns it into heat. The sign is negative because the force and the displacement point in opposite directions.

questions.q: On a graph of force (y-axis) versus displacement (x-axis), what does the area under the curve represent?
o: Impulse is the area under force versus time.
Power is work per unit time.
Momentum change comes from F–t area.
questions.x: Work is force times displacement, so the area under an F–x graph is work. This works even when the force varies, for example with a spring. The area under an F–t graph is impulse instead. Checking units (N × m = J) tells them apart.

questions.q: How much work is needed to stretch a spring (k = 200 N/m) from its natural length to 0.1 m?
o: Uses kx (the force) as the work.
Takes half the final force (½kx = 10 N) as the work.
questions.x: A spring's force rises steadily from 0 to kx, so the work is the area of a triangle: ½kx² = ½ × 200 × 0.01 = 1 J. That is the same as the average force (10 N) times the distance (0.1 m). Using the final force kx for the whole stretch overestimates the work.

questions.q: A spring (k = 200 N/m) is already stretched 0.1 m. How much additional work stretches it to 0.2 m?
o: That is the work for the first 0.1 m only.
That is the total work from 0 to 0.2 m.
Assumes each 0.1 m costs the same, ignoring the rising force.
questions.note: Spring work grows with x², not x.
questions.x: Spring energy grows with x², so later stretching costs more. The work from 0.1 m to 0.2 m is ½k(x₂² − x₁²) = 100 × 0.03 = 3 J, three times the 1 J needed for the first 0.1 m. Assuming equal steps cost equal work ignores that the force keeps rising.

questions.q: According to the work–energy theorem, the net work done on an object equals its change in:
o: Conservative work equals −ΔPE, not net work.
questions.x: The work–energy theorem says the work done by all forces together equals the change in kinetic energy: W_net = ΔKE. Conservative forces' work can instead be written as −ΔPE. Work done by nonconservative forces such as friction changes the total mechanical energy, not the net-work relationship.

questions.q: A weightlifter holds a 20 kg barbell motionless overhead for 30 s. How much mechanical work does she do on the barbell?
o: Zero, although her muscles still consume ATP
Correct: no displacement means no work on the barbell; muscle fibers spend energy cycling.
Multiplies force by time; work needs displacement.
That is the weight in newtons, not work.
Negative work, since gravity pulls down
With no displacement, neither force does work.
questions.x: Mechanical work requires displacement along the force (W = Fd cos θ). The barbell does not move, so no work is done on it. Her muscles still use ATP, because cross-bridges keep cycling to maintain tension, and that energy ends up as heat. Physical work and metabolic cost are different things.

questions.q: A force sensor shows force rising linearly from 0 to 40 N as an object moves 0.5 m. How much work was done?
o: Uses the maximum force for the whole distance.
questions.x: When force varies, work is the area under the F–x graph. A linear rise from 0 to 40 N over 0.5 m makes a triangle: ½ × 40 × 0.5 = 10 J. Using the peak force for the whole distance doubles the answer, because the average force is only 20 N.

questions.q: The left ventricle ejects 70 mL of blood against an average pressure of about 13 kPa (≈ 100 mmHg). About how much work is done per beat?
o: Off by 10 in converting mL to m³.
Correct: W = PΔV = 13,000 Pa × 70 × 10⁻⁶ m³ ≈ 0.91 J.
questions.note: 1 mL = 10⁻⁶ m³.
questions.x: Pumping fluid against a pressure does work W = PΔV. Converting the volume, 70 mL = 70 × 10⁻⁶ m³, gives W = 13,000 × 7 × 10⁻⁵ ≈ 0.9 J per beat. The key conversion is 1 mL = 1 cm³ = 10⁻⁶ m³. Each power-of-ten slip changes the answer tenfold.

questions.q: An object's speed triples. By what factor does its kinetic energy change?
o: Correct: KE = ½mv², so KE ∝ v².
Doubles the factor of 3 instead of squaring it.
questions.x: Kinetic energy is ½mv², so it grows with the square of speed. Tripling v multiplies KE by 3² = 9. Momentum, mv, would only triple. That is why higher speeds are disproportionately dangerous.

questions.q: What is the kinetic energy of a 0.2 kg ball moving at 10 m/s?
o: That is the momentum value, mv.
questions.x: KE = ½mv² = ½ × 0.2 × 10² = 10 J. Remember to square the velocity and to include the ½. The value mv = 2 kg·m/s is the momentum, a different quantity with different units.

questions.q: Two objects have equal momentum, but one has twice the mass of the other. What is the ratio of their kinetic energies (heavier : lighter)?
o: Assumes the heavier object has more KE at equal momentum.
Correct: KE = p²/2m, so at equal p, KE ∝ 1/m.
Equal momentum doesn't mean equal KE.
questions.x: Combining p = mv and KE = ½mv² gives KE = p²/(2m). With equal momentum, KE is inversely proportional to mass, so the heavier object has half the KE (1 : 2). It moves at half the speed, and speed enters KE squared.

questions.q: A 70 kg climber ascends 100 m. What is the increase in her gravitational potential energy (g = 10 m/s²)?
o: Forgets the height factor or g.
questions.x: The change in gravitational potential energy is ΔU = mgh = 70 × 10 × 100 = 70,000 J (70 kJ). Near Earth's surface, U changes linearly with height. Counting powers of ten carefully avoids the factor-of-10 distractors.

questions.q: A spring is compressed twice as far as before. By what factor does its stored elastic potential energy change?
questions.x: Elastic potential energy is U = ½kx², so it grows with the square of the compression. Doubling x stores 2² = 4 times the energy. The spring force, kx, only doubles, but energy is the area under the force curve, which grows as x².

questions.q: Moving the zero level of gravitational potential energy from the floor to a tabletop changes which of the following?
o: Shifting the reference adds a constant that cancels in ΔU.
The value of U at each point, but not ΔU between two points
Correct: only differences in potential energy are physical.
The reference choice has no effect on KE.
questions.x: Potential energy is defined only relative to a reference level you choose. Moving the zero adds the same constant to U everywhere, so the differences, ΔU, stay the same. Only ΔU affects forces, work and motion, so physical predictions do not depend on the choice.

questions.q: A spring (k = 400 N/m) compressed 0.05 m launches a 0.1 kg block across a frictionless surface. What is the block's speed?
o: Drops the ½ in KE: mv² = 0.5 J gives v² = 5.
Uses force kx = 20 N as a speed.
Correct: ½kx² = 0.5 J; ½(0.1)v² = 0.5 gives v² = 10.
questions.x: Stored spring energy becomes kinetic energy: ½kx² = ½ × 400 × 0.0025 = 0.5 J. Then ½(0.1)v² = 0.5, so v² = 10 and v ≈ 3.2 m/s. Remember to take the square root at the end and to keep the ½ on both sides.

questions.q: Which of the following forces is nonconservative?
o: Correct: friction's work depends on path and turns mechanical energy into heat.
Gravity's work depends only on endpoints.
Spring work depends only on endpoints.
Electrostatic work depends only on endpoints.
questions.x: A force is conservative if its work depends only on the start and end points, so it does zero work around any closed loop. Gravity, ideal springs and electrostatic forces meet this test, so each has a potential energy. Kinetic friction does more work the longer the path and always takes mechanical energy away as heat.

questions.q: During running, the Achilles tendon (effective k ≈ 2 × 10⁵ N/m) stretches about 1 cm. How much elastic energy does it store?
o: Uses x = 0.1 m instead of 0.01 m.
Uses kx (the force) as the energy.
questions.note: Tendons return stored energy, improving running economy.
questions.x: A spring stores energy U = ½kx². With x = 0.01 m, x² = 10⁻⁴ m², so U = ½ × 2 × 10⁵ × 10⁻⁴ = 10 J. Convert centimeters to meters before squaring: leaving x as 0.1 m inflates the answer 100-fold. Using kx gives the tendon force in newtons, not an energy.

questions.q: A rock is dropped from rest off a 45 m cliff. Ignoring air resistance, how fast is it moving just before impact (g = 10 m/s²)?
questions.x: Energy conservation gives mgh = ½mv², so v = √(2gh) = √(2 × 10 × 45) = 30 m/s. Mass cancels. The kinematics formula v² = 2gh gives the same result. Dropping the 2 or forgetting the final square root are the usual slips.

questions.q: A roller coaster car starts from rest 30 m above the ground. Ignoring friction, what is its speed when it is 10 m above the ground (g = 10 m/s²)?
o: Correct: drop of 20 m; v = √(2 × 10 × 20) = 20 m/s.
questions.note: Only the height dropped matters.
questions.x: Only the height dropped turns into kinetic energy. The car falls 30 − 10 = 20 m, so v = √(2gh) = √400 = 20 m/s. Using the full 30 m height pretends the car reached the ground. The shape of the track does not matter without friction.

questions.q: A 50 kg sledder starts from rest at the top of a 10 m high hill and reaches 10 m/s at the bottom. How much energy was lost to friction (g = 10 m/s²)?
o: Correct: mgh = 5000 J; KE = ½(50)(100) = 2500 J; lost 2500 J.
That is the total initial PE.
Adds KE to PE instead of subtracting.
The final KE is less than the initial PE, so energy was dissipated.
questions.x: Energy at the start is mgh = 50 × 10 × 10 = 5000 J. At the bottom, KE = ½ × 50 × 10² = 2500 J. The missing 2500 J was turned into heat by friction (W_friction = −2500 J). Energy lost is always the difference between the initial and final mechanical energy.

questions.q: Two identical balls are thrown from the same rooftop at the same speed, one horizontally and one straight down. Ignoring air resistance, how do their speeds compare just before they land?
o: Correct: same initial KE and same PE drop give the same final KE.
Direction of launch doesn't change energy.
Both gain the same KE from the same drop.
Mass cancels in the energy equation.
questions.x: Kinetic energy is a scalar, so the launch direction does not matter. Both balls start with the same KE and drop the same height, so they gain the same energy and land at the same speed. The ball thrown downward lands sooner, but not faster.

questions.q: A horizontal mass–spring system oscillates on a frictionless surface. At the equilibrium position, which quantity is at its maximum?
o: Spring PE is maximum at the turning points.
Correct: spring PE is zero there, so all mechanical energy is kinetic.
questions.x: At equilibrium, x = 0, so the spring force (−kx), the acceleration and the elastic PE (½kx²) are all zero. All the mechanical energy is then kinetic, so the speed is greatest. At the turning points it is the reverse: maximum PE, force and acceleration, and zero speed.

questions.q: A ball dropped from 2.0 m rebounds to 1.5 m. What fraction of its mechanical energy was lost in the bounce?
o: Correct: PE ∝ height, and the height fell from 2.0 to 1.5 m.
Assumes energy halves with each bounce.
Uses the square root of the height ratio (a speed ratio).
questions.x: Gravitational PE is proportional to height, so the fraction of energy kept is 1.5/2.0 = 75%. That means 25% was lost to heat and sound in the bounce. Using the square root of the height ratio gives a speed ratio, not an energy ratio.

questions.q: A cart rolls down a 2 m ramp, losing 4.0 J of gravitational PE, and has 3.2 J of kinetic energy at the bottom. What is the average friction force along the ramp?
o: Gives the energy lost, not the force.
Multiplies the lost energy by distance.
Divides the full 4.0 J of PE by the distance.
questions.x: Of the 4.0 J of PE lost, only 3.2 J became KE, so friction removed 0.8 J. Friction work is force × distance, so f = 0.8 J ÷ 2 m = 0.4 N. Dividing the full 4.0 J by the distance treats all the PE as lost to friction.

questions.q: Total mechanical energy of a system is conserved when:
o: Net force can be nonzero (e.g., free fall) while energy is conserved.
Any friction dissipates some mechanical energy.
The object moves at constant speed
A block sliding at constant speed down a rough ramp loses mechanical energy.
Correct: nonconservative forces (friction, drag) convert mechanical energy to other forms.
questions.x: Mechanical energy (KE + PE) stays constant when only conservative forces, such as gravity and springs, do work. Friction, drag and muscles do nonconservative work and change it. A nonzero net force is fine: in free fall gravity is the net force, yet mechanical energy is conserved.

questions.q: A pole vaulter runs at 10 m/s. If all of her kinetic energy became gravitational PE, how high could she raise her center of mass (g = 10 m/s²)?
questions.note: Mass cancels in v²/2g.
questions.x: Setting ½mv² = mgh gives h = v²/(2g) = 100/20 = 5 m. Mass cancels, so the speed alone sets the ideal height. Real vaulters clear about 6 m because their center of mass starts about 1 m above the ground and they push with their arms.

questions.q: A pendulum with a 1.8 m string is released from rest at 60° from vertical. What is its speed at the lowest point (g = 10 m/s²)?
o: Uses the full string length as the height drop.
Uses h = 0.45 m, half the true drop.
questions.x: The bob drops h = L − L cos θ = 1.8(1 − 0.5) = 0.9 m. Then v = √(2gh) = √18 ≈ 4.2 m/s. The tricky step is the geometry: the vertical drop is L(1 − cos θ), not L and not L sin θ.

questions.q: A block slides down a rough incline at constant speed. What happens to its mechanical energy?
o: It stays constant because speed is constant
Constant KE but falling PE means total mechanical energy drops.
It increases as PE turns into KE
KE doesn't increase at constant speed.
It decreases as thermal energy is produced
Correct: PE drops while KE stays constant; friction converts the difference to heat.
It is converted entirely into kinetic energy
questions.x: Constant speed means KE does not change, but the block keeps losing height and therefore PE. So the total mechanical energy goes down, and kinetic friction turns the lost PE into thermal energy. Constant speed means the forces balance; it does not mean energy is conserved.

questions.q: In a lab, a solid ball rolling without slipping down a ramp consistently has about 30% less translational KE at the bottom than mgh predicts. What best explains this?
o: The ball's mass was too large
Mass cancels in comparing KE to mgh.
The local value of g is larger than assumed
A larger g would increase the KE.
Some energy goes into the ball's rotational kinetic energy
Correct: for a solid sphere, 2/7 of the energy (≈ 29%) is rotational.
Underestimating h would make KE seem too large.
questions.x: A ball rolling without slipping has to spin as well as move forward. Part of mgh becomes rotational KE (½Iω²), so less is left for translational KE. For a solid sphere, I = ⅖mr², so 2/7 (≈29%) of the energy goes into rotation, which matches the data. Mass cancels, so mass cannot be the explanation.
